messages.subject: colext with (some) missing season data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I hope you are having an excellent Labor Day weekend.

I'm running colext models for a two-year dataset.  Unfortunately, not all sites were visited in both years; 244 one year, 266 the next, 95 in both, 415 sites altogether.

My first thought was that the only valid sites in which to model colext were the 95 sites sampled in both years.  However, the models ran fine when with the full set of 415 sites.  Occupancy and detection parameter estimates were somewhat different (as expected, using different sites) between the two (95 'complete' vs. 415 w/ missing data).  It surprised me that the 415-site model had different colonization and extinction parameter estimates than the 95-site model as (I reason, probably incorrectly) both models were working with the same subset of sites common to both years.

Like anyone, I'm hoping for a more robust sample; is the sample of 415 sites valid, despite some sites not being visited in subsequent (or initial) years?

Thanks, as always.   Giancarlo

The choices might be 415 vs. 0 rather than 415 vs. 95.  If the three sets of data were taken as a random sample from the same population of sites and the choice of the years to survey was not dependent on status in any one year (or on previous years as there are some who like to sample more often from sites more likely to have detections - without accounting for that), then I'd say use all 415.

If the determination of which years to sample is more on the "selected without a randomization scheme" side (for whatever reason was used for the uneven sampling), then I'd side with the sample size of 0.

I am being a bit facetious in the previous paragraphs but I think the decision has to do solely with how you performed the sampling (selection of sites and which years were surveyed for those sites) rather than if the results differ (although wildly differing results would be consistent with non-random selection issues) between the 415 and 95 analyses.

How were the sites selected and the years to be surveyed determined?

messages.body_plain:
For whatever it's worth, I agree:  there are no problems with missing data for computing results.  However, if the missing site*year combinations are not missing at random, then there can be issues with the model not being a valid description of the actual data collection process.

For example, if some sites in a forest become too dangerous to revisit because of armed agroforestry operations, then those sites might also be very different from the remaining sites.  Same thing when one runs out of money and can't survey the more-expensive-to-get-to sites or the high elevation sites couldn't be surveyed because the snow hasn't yet melted.

In summary, one can obtain estimates with lots of missing data but if that "missingness" has something to do with the type of sites not surveyed or the desire to visit sites more likely to have detections (not at all suggesting that's the case here), then missingness is a problem.

Jim Baldwin

Hello, I have some questions regarding the best analysis approach for my data.

Goal:
Estimate lizard densities and the effect of habitat covariates on lizard densities

Data:
223 line transects with distance measurements for each animal
covariates measured at either the transect (site-level) or at the forest-fragment level

2) Transect surveys are repeated in one (and only one) of the forest fragments in a different season.

Analysis options:
1) regarding random effects
    a) Ignore random effects: treat transects as fully independent, even if they occur in the same forest fragment.
    b) Average all site-level covariates to the forest-fragment scale (transects & covariate measurements were placed randomly within each fragment)
    c) estimate density at each site without covariates & then use GLMM to model density estimates as a function of covariates
2) regarding semi-repeated surveys:
    a) Include season as covariate  (with a random effect for fragment, I think this would be the easy solution)
    b) exclude 2nd season from main analysis & run 2nd analysis with both seasons, but only the forest fragment that has surveys from both seasons

I'm not sure how to weight the pros/cons of these approaches, so I welcome any suggests you may have.

Thanks,
Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Lance,

It will generally be the case that if you change the model for one of the parameters (lambda, phi, or p), it will affect the estimates of the others. For example, think about the different abundance estimates you might get in models with and without an important covariate of detection probability.

I can't explain the results you are seeing for your specific dataset, but the reason for the density estimator given in our Ecology paper is that we considered the case where lambda is the expected size of the super-population (the number of individuals that could have used the plot during the sampling period). You can't just divide lambda by area because the super-population is associated with an area larger than the plot area. However, under random temporary emigration, the number of individuals expected to occur on the plot during a short time period is E[N] = lambda*phi, so density is E[N]/area. Note that this estimator does not apply to situations where "availability" is related to processes other than temporary emigration. i.e. the interpretation of phi is specific to the study and species.

Richard

Hi all, some general advice would be greatly appreciated!

We have a dataset of Yellow-billed Cuckoo surveys (4 visits at 1400 points in riparian habitat), but a seemingly fatal issue is that we have very few detections and zero repeat detections. We'd like to run a standard single season occupancy model to get a rough estimate of the number of territories in our study area. So that the occupancy metric is on scale with territory size we planned on aggregating adjacent point count locations at a range of sizes approximating the territory size of the species.

YBCU is an episodic and cryptic species (may or may not call when close to field observers). There were a total of 9 detections. But even with the largest aggregation of point count locations that we identified a priori, none of the sampling units had any repeat detections. The detections are just too far apart and we feel they are in fact different individuals so it would not really be appropriate to aggregate at that scale. Can we still fit an occupancy model without any repeat detections?

One possibility in these data is that all nine detections were from birds not associated with territories, the could simply all be 'drifters' that are un-paired and not breeding?

> > > > You don't need multiple visits to estimate occupancy. If you assume a
> > > > Poisson distribution for abundance at each site, you can compute

> > > > # function to simulate dependent double observer data
> > > > sim.dep.double <- function(nSites=200, numPrimary=2, lambda=1, phi=0.6,
> > > >                            pA=0.8, pB=0.6, alpha=0.5)
> > > > {
> > >
> > > >     N <- matrix(NA, nSites, numPrimary)
> > > >     y <- array(NA, c(nSites, 2, numPrimary))
> > >
> > > >     # Abundance at each site
> > > >     M <- rnbinom(nSites, size=alpha, mu=lambda)
> > >
> > > >     # Number available during each rep
> > > >     for(i in 1:nSites) {
> > > >         N[i,] <- rbinom(numPrimary, M[i], phi)
> > > >         }
> > >
> > > >     # Number observed
> > > >     for(i in 1:nSites) {
> > > >         for(t in 1:numPrimary) {
> > > >             cp <- c(pA, pB * (1 - pA))
> > > >             cp[3] <- 1 - sum(cp)
> > > >             y[i,,t] <- c(rmultinom(1, N[i,t], cp)[1:2])

Dear Users,
                   I've been using N-mixture models to perform some preliminary analysis of fecundity in a single season. I have only two repeated observations across 43 sites.
 Because some colonies can have kits and some not I thought a ZIP model would be appropriate. This way I could model detection, and for abundance (or number of kits in this case), whether the colonies produce or not kits at one level, and how many kits at the other level. 2) The probability of detection decreases drastically.
3) I would like to introduce covariates to model abundance at the the two levels (production and number of kits). Is this possible?

Any suggestion regarding these points will be appreciated.

Alejandro

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] overdispersion in pcount models: QAIC?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I’m in a similar position trying to get at overdispersion. I’m working with a pcount Poisson model for abundance and detection probability of juvenile coho salmon in pools of Oregon streams.  Estimates from the negative binomial models wouldn’t ever settle as I increased initial K values, so I’ve stuck with Poisson.  My models don’t seem to have great fit, and I’d like to be able to consider and account for overdispersion.  To get at this, I’ve calculated the deviance residuals from observed and expected (fitted function) counts. I then took the sum of the squared deviance residuals and divided by the degrees of freedom to calculate a dispersion parameter with which to adjust my AIC and SE values.  I’ve included the code below.  The equations I took from stats courses and books.

After running this code, I do get a dispersion parameter that’s roughly similar to dispersion from a quasipoisson glm on just the abundance model, and also similar to Suresh’s Chi-squared-derived dispersion parameter.  (Unfortunately, the dispersion parameters are all disconcertingly high, ranging from around 4.5-6.5 for models in three different streams.)  In any case, everything in the code seems to function just fine, but I’d very much like a second, more experienced opinion on the appropriateness of using this method for pcount Poisson models in unmarked.

Your thoughts and advice are much appreciated!  Please let me know if you have any questions for me.

Kristen

Code:

full.model<-pcount(~diver.h+areap.h+depthp.h+woody.h~depth.h+area.h+ddf.h+cd.h,K=350,h.umf)

k<-10    # number of parameters

observed <- getY(full.model@data)

expected <- fitted(full.model)

df<-(length(observed)-sum(is.na <http://is.na>(observed)))-k  #degrees of freedom

dev.i<-(sign(observed-expected)*sqrt(2*(observed*log(observed/expected)-(observed-expected))))  # Individual deviance residuals

dev.i.sq<-dev.i^2

sumsqdev<-sum(dev.i.sq,na.rm=T) #sum of squared residuals

dispersion<-sumsqdev/df

c.hat<-dispersion   # c.hat / dispersion parameter

q.aic.m1<-(-2*logLik(full.model)/c.hat)+(2*k*(k+1)/(n-k-1)) #Quasi-AICc

# Adjusted SE and P-values

se.full.model<-SE(full.model)

se.adj<-((sqrt(c.hat))*se.full.model)

z.adj<-(coef(full.model)/se.adj)

p.adj<-2*pnorm(-abs(z.adj))

> Dear ‘unmarked’ gurus,
>
> I’m attempting to model the influence of habitat variables on
> occurrence and detection for juvenile salmon in lake habitats using a
> Royle N-mixture model for repeated minnow trapping counts (pcount() in
> unmarked).  The global model suggests overdispersion from a Poisson
> state process model (likely from schooling of fish), as assessed by a
> parametric bootstrap goodness of fit testing procedure using a Chi-
> squared fit statistic (Fiske and Chandler 2011; MacKenzie and Bailey
> 2004).
>
> From my understanding, there’s a few options to deal with
> overdispersion in this context which could be implemented with
> ‘unmarked’:
> 1. Accommodate overdispersion by modeling the state process as
> Negative Binomial.
> 2. Accommodate overdispersion using ZIP state process.
>
> And my question to you:
> 3. Use a Poisson state process, but adjust model inference using a
> variance inflation factor (e.g. QAIC, and assuming that one believes
> their model is structurally sufficient to characterize expected
> abundance but that they wish to get more honest estimates of
> coefficient uncertainty).
>
> I’ve implemented options 1 and 2, but they are not satisfactory in
> this case (NB model passes par. boot. g.o.f. test but very sensitive
> to choice of K parameter for integrated likelihood; ZIP model
> demonstrates systematic upward bias in residuals for predicted
> abundance whereas models with Poisson and NB state processes show no
> such bias).  In particular I would appreciate your comment on the use
> of QAIC for Royle N-mixture models on repeated counts (single-season,
> pcount() type model).
>
> Could one extend the thinking of MacKenzie and Bailey (2004) and White
> et al. (2002) to come up with an estimate of a (constant) variance
> inflation factor for use in a repeated count N-mixture model
> application using a parametric bootstrap routine (e.g. code provided
> in Fiske and Chandler 2011) and a Chi square fit statistic as:
> c.hat = (observed.chi.sq.stat)/mean(par.boot.chi.sq.stats)?
> Regarding such an estimate of c.hat, White et al. (2002, pg. 375)
> summarize the spirit of this approach: "The logic is that the mean of
> the simulated deviances represents the expected value of the deviance
> under the null model of no violations of assumptions (i.e., perfect
> fit of the model to the data). Thus, cˆ = observed deviance divided by
> expected deviance provides a measure of the amount of overdispersion
> in the original data."
>
> Thanks for your comments, and thanks for writing and maintaining the
> very impressive 'unmarked' package.
>
> Cheers,
>
> Suresh Andrew Sethi
> US Fish and Wildlife Service, Alaska
